newsitem.title: UK: UK rate rise seen possible, but unlikely, tomorrow.
newsitem.headline: UK rate rise seen possible, but unlikely, tomorrow.

text.p: The Bank of England did not provide conclusive evidence in its money market operations on Wednesday that interest rates had been left unchanged after the monetary meeting and it could announce a rate rise on Thursday morning.
But economists said this was highly unlikely and they expect the opening round of operations at around 0945 GMT on Thursday to show official rates on hold at 6.0 percent.

"Whether they will be left unchanged tomorrow is a leap of faith," said John Shepperd, chief UK economist at Yamaichi International. "One assumes they will be, but we need to see tomorrow's operations for confirmation."

Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke and Bank of England Governor Eddie George were still holding their monthly monetary meeting when the Bank conducted its first round of operations just after 1200 GMT.
It bought bills at an unchanged rate of 5-15/16 percent.
The Bank dealt at the same rate in the 1400 GMT round, indicating that no change would take place on Wednesday.

"The Bank will not deal at two different rates during the course of the day," said Philip Shaw, chief economist at Union Plc. "Having already operated at midday, it would be highly unusual for it to deal at a different rate."
"For the official signal of the result of the meeting, we will have to wait until 0945 tomorrow morning," Shaw added. "I would be very surprised if rates were to move."

Some market participants interpreted a fairly innocuous lunchtime television interview with Clarke, in which he said George would announce the outcome of the meeting in due course, as a signal that rates would be raised.
But the Treasury quickly denied this, saying his comments should not be construed as a pointer in any direction.
Clarke and George have been at odds over monetary policy since the December 11 monetary meeting.

The Governor, who fears inflation is set to pick up in the next 18 months or so, argued unsuccessfully for an immediate quarter-point rise to 6.25 percent and warned that he would otherwise probably advise a half-point rise in January or February.
Clarke, who has a strong political incentive not to raise rates in the run-up to an election, said the economic signals were mixed and the case had not been made for tightening policy.
The Chancellor has since said that the economic data, including unexpected falls in manufacturing output and retail sales, have "gone his way."
Clarke has also said that the strength of sterling would dampen inflationary pressures, an argument publicly rejected by George.
Both men are likely to have seen December manufacturing output data, to be released on Thursday morning. The market consensus is for a bounceback after November's fall.

In a Reuters survey conducted last Friday, 23 out of 24 economists said they expected no change in rates from Wednesday's meeting. Most believe Clarke will leave rates on hold until after the election, due by May 22 at the latest.
